historical_observations: The rounded Say column gives a full span of 7.4 ft and a wrist-to-wrist span of 3.7 ft.
The paragraph gives the original total wing area as 6.61 square feet.
The pictured inner wing is broadly parallel-chord and the outer wing tapers.
The text distinguishes an inner arm wing from an articulated outer hand wing.
The manoeuvring discussion recommends a conventional tail or weight shift for an elementary ornithopter.
The tail discussion says a fin or rudder would probably benefit an ornithopter.

implementation: Each wing has a rigid parallel-chord inner panel and tapered outer panel hinged at its wrist.
The wrist hinges are 1.5 m apart and complete tip-to-tip span is 3.0 m.
A crank articulates both inner panels; each outer panel changes angle relative to its inner panel.
A horizontal tail, elevator, fin and input-driven rudder translate source 14's control suggestion.

engineering_assumptions.status: Proposed benchmark assumptions for review, not historical observations or measured aircraft data.
engineering_assumptions.drive_and_structure: Electric motor, crank, pin-jointed spars, triangulated frame and rolling tricycle gear are new visual engineering choices.
engineering_assumptions.flight_model: Cycle-averaged point-mass translation with the specified educational polar, power conversion, rudder side force and commanded attitude rates.

excluded_fields.reason: Explicitly identified as erroneous and not used.
Unavailable or explicitly excluded; the original 6.61 square-foot area is used.

excluded_fields.item: animal body width, neck and overall length
excluded_fields.reason: Biological dimensions do not prescribe the mechanical fuselage.

excluded_fields.item: exact biological stroke angles, spring stiffness and curved-plate polar
excluded_fields.reason: Reference frames or quantitative data are incomplete.
It is insufficiently quantified for this educational force model.

limitations: The cycle-averaged aerodynamic model omits blade-element, wake, stall hysteresis, aeroelastic and inertial wing loads.
Geometry communicates the mechanism, while translation uses benchmark equations rather than mesh-integrated moving-panel forces.
Ground support uses vertical point contacts; tire compliance, suspension, wheel inertia and terrain-normal forces are omitted.
Attitude follows bounded educational control rates rather than rigid-body moments.
This shared-world model is not evidence of practical flight performance or safety.
